title: Dry-Hole Atlas for Hydrogen, Helium, Geothermal
one_liner: Re-read a century of scanned well logs and gas analyses, once treated as junk, to find natural hydrogen, helium and hot rock, and sell the resulting atlas to exploration companies by area of interest.
customer: Junior exploration companies and VC-backed developers in natural hydrogen, helium and geothermal (and lithium-brine plays), plus land and mineral-lease advisors who need leads. They pay for subscriptions and area-of-interest data packs.
problem: The US has millions of drilled wells. Old records include gas analyses, bottom-hole temperatures, water chemistry and mud-log shows, mostly recorded as incidental noise by oil and gas operators. They sit as scanned TIFFs and PDFs at state geological surveys and core repositories. New subsurface commodities need exactly this once-discarded information. Oil-and-gas data vendors index hydrocarbon fields, not hydrogen, helium or heat, and small explorers cannot afford to hire teams to dig through archives across 30 state surveys.
solution: A scan-to-structured-data pipeline across public state survey archives. Extract gas composition (hydrogen, helium, nitrogen), bottom-hole temperature and depth, and brine chemistry. Geolocate every record, correct for known temperature-log biases, and publish a queryable map atlas with prospectivity layers per township or section. Sell by area of interest. Offer custom queries such as 'every well within 20 miles of this substation with more than 0.3% helium and temperature above 150 C at 3 km'.
why_now: AI data centers are driving huge demand for clean firm power, and geothermal developers are raising large rounds and signing hyperscaler offtakes. Natural hydrogen exploration has attracted venture money and government attention. Helium supply has been unstable and prices volatile. Vision-language models now extract tables from old scans cheaply, and state surveys are increasingly open to releasing data.
revenue_model: Subscriptions of 15-50k USD per year per company for a basin or state atlas, area-of-interest packs of 5-25k USD, custom data services, and, later, small overriding royalties or success fees on leases won using the data.
non_obvious_insight: The value of data flips when the target commodity changes. A well that reported 'gas contains 40% hydrogen' in 1935 was a dud then, and it is a discovery lead today. Every incumbent data vendor is organized around the old commodity, so nobody re-reads the archive for byproducts. The archives are public and low-margin for the state agencies that hold them, so the moat is the extraction pipeline, cleaning and geological calibration, not data access.
first_30_days: Pick one state survey with well-documented public scans and gas-analysis reports and one target commodity (helium or hydrogen shows are the easiest to demo). Build a proof-of-concept map for one basin using a few thousand well records. Cold-email about 30 junior exploration companies and geothermal developers with the map and one concrete lead they can check. Sell 3-5 area-of-interest packs at around 5k USD each, and ask for pre-payment for the next state.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: USGS/BLM Natural Gas Compositional Analyses Dataset (free), USGS Geologic Hydrogen Prospectivity Map Explorer, SMU / NGDS heat-flow and corrected bottom-hole-temperature database (now on the DOE Geothermal Data Repository), Project InnerSpace GeoMap. White space: The wedge that remains is narrow but real. Nobody found sells page-level, provenance-linked hydrogen, helium and heat evidence extracted from the unstructured parts of old well files. That means mud-log gas shows, drill-stem-test and production-test reports, driller notes such as non-flammable gas, and water-well gas, all at lease-block or section level. The free datasets (USGS/BLM, SMU/GDR, KGS) already cover the structured gas-analysis and corrected-BHT layers, so a paid product cannot rest on those. The USGS roughly 16,000 He-bearing points and the 30,000 corrected BHT wells are a free baseline that any paid product has to beat. The Paris Basin OCR study found only 26 wells with H2 detection out of about 5,000 in the database (0.5%), which suggests few real leads per basin. Unserved specifics: (1) the 20-30 state and provincial archives whose scans are not yet digitized, with a defensible per-record confidence grade (sampling method, air contamination, analytical era); (2) one integrated He, H2 and heat layer, where the players found each cover a single commodity; (3) delivery to small juniors, landmen and lease advisors who cannot fund in-house teams. Koloma, Zanskar, HyTerra and MAX Power already do this in-house, so the addressable buyers are the smaller players (AKAP counts 123 companies in natural hydrogen, Rystad counted 40) plus the lease and land side.

title: Aftermarket Support for Stranded DJI Fleets
one_liner: Repair, rebuilt batteries, parts and firmware-independence retrofits for the many legally owned DJI drones that can no longer be replaced with new models.
customer: Police and fire drone units, agricultural spray operators, land surveyors, roofing and solar inspectors, and small public-safety departments with grant money.
problem: The FCC barred new DJI and Autel models in December 2025, US drone tariffs took effect in September 2026 (component tariffs follow in 2027), and China's export controls now cover motors, batteries, radios and sensors. Existing fleets stay legal to fly but face scarce parts and no assured US repair path.
solution: A US repair depot with stocked parts, rebuilt batteries using allied-source cells, gimbal and camera swaps, and open flight-controller retrofits (ArduPilot/PX4) as a migration path. Offer a per-drone maintenance plan with predictive service, and trade-in credits toward US-made airframes, which also become a lead source for those makers.
why_now: The December 2025 FCC action, September 2026 tariffs and export controls all landed within a year. The installed base is large and aging, and no one has a business focused on serving it.
revenue_model: $150-800 per repair, $30-80 per drone per month for maintenance plans, battery and parts sales, and referral fees from US airframe makers on trade-ins.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone debates who replaces DJI, while nobody serves the installed base for the next 5 years. Service earns higher margin than building a competing airframe, starts faster, and gives you the customer list every US-made airframe maker wants.
first_30_days: Buy 20 broken Mavic and Matrice units on secondary markets and set up a bench. Pitch fixed-price maintenance plans to 30 sheriff drone units and agricultural spraying co-ops, and sell the first 10 plans.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: DJI (own repair, DJI Care, Authorized Service Centers via CarePro Technology Inc), Drone Nerds (plus Drone Nerds Enterprise), Dronefly, BRINC (Safeguard Program). White space: The claim that nobody serves the installed base is wrong. DJI/CarePro, Drone Nerds, Dronefly and small independents already repair DJI drones, and Drone Nerds already sells enterprise hot-swap and always-flying plans. The gap is capacity and guaranteed turnaround. Repair waits reportedly went from days to about three months (https://dronexl.co/2026/09/01/fcc-covered-list-panel-uav-expo-repair-times/), and replacement hardware takes 6-9 weeks. What looks unserved: (1) A US depot with a real SLA (about 72 hours) and loaner pools for Matrice, Mavic 3 Enterprise and Agras spray fleets, sold as overflow capacity to backlogged authorized centers and resellers as well as directly. (2) Agricultural spray operators: DJI has roughly 80% of US spray-drone sales and cumulative tariffs have tripled prices (about $20k to $100k), so these fleets have no affordable replacement (https://dronexl.co/2025/12/17/connecticut-ag-drone-law-tariffs-ban/). FCC docket 26-189 also targets economic-poison spraying drones for retroactive action. (3) Rebuilt batteries from allied-source cells: I found no one doing this at scale, but DJI smart-battery lockouts make it technically uncertain, and I could not check that. (4) Parts stockpiling ahead of the component tariffs that start 2027-02-09. (5) Buying retired fleets from agencies that are switching, for refurbish, resale and parts harvest; El Paso's chief said the department will dispose of its DJI equipment once replacements arrive. The open ArduPilot/PX4 retrofit has no precedent or demand signal that I found. It also does not remove the DJI camera, gimbal and radio modules, so it does not fix compliance. It is the weakest part of the idea.

title: Contingency Audit of Unbilled Plumbing Materials
one_liner: Reconcile a trade shop's supply-house invoices against its customer invoices and catch both parts that were bought but never billed and quiet supplier price drift, paid a percentage of what gets recovered.
customer: Plumbing, HVAC and electrical shops doing $1.5-15M in revenue with 5-40 techs, running ServiceTitan, Housecall Pro or Jobber plus QuickBooks, buying on account from Ferguson, Hajoca, Winsupply or a local supply house.
problem: Shops lose margin in two places nobody watches. First, parts go out on a supply-house ticket with a job name, or come off the truck stock, and never make it onto the customer invoice. Techs charge the labor from the flat-rate book and forget the $6 valve, the wax ring, the supply lines, the $40 of fittings. In the shops I know, when the office finally reconciles a quarter it is typically a few percent of revenue. Second, supply houses price off list with a contractor multiplier, and list prices have moved several times since the Section 232 copper, steel and aluminum tariffs (50%, working through a long manufacturer-to-contractor lag). Surcharges appear, job-quoted prices are not honored, returns credits are never issued, and no owner has time to read 40 invoices a week.
solution: Shops set up an email forwarding rule for supply-house invoices and statements and give us read access to their field-service software export. An LLM-based line-item parser ties supply-house lines to jobs and POs, then produces a weekly leak list for the office manager: (1) purchased-not-billed by job, (2) price versus the shop's own multiplier and versus the same SKU 30 days ago, (3) unclaimed return credits, (4) pricebook items where cost has risen past the target markup, with a repricing file ready to import. Later add a benchmark ('you pay 9% more than shops your size for PEX-A fittings') built from pooled anonymized invoices, which is the moat.
why_now: Tariff-driven price volatility means flat-rate pricebooks are stale within a quarter, and owners know it. Invoice parsing with LLMs went from a custom-ML project to an afternoon. Field-service platforms expose APIs and exports. The trades are also ahead of everyone else in adopting software but behind in auditing it, so there is no incumbent audit product.
revenue_model: Contingency fee of 25% of recovered and newly captured revenue for the first 12 months (no recovery, no fee), converting to a $199-499 per month subscription for continuous monitoring plus the pricing benchmark. Data licensing of the pooled price index to distributors and manufacturers later.
non_obvious_insight: Owners obsess over lead cost and tech hiring while the highest-ROI dollar is sitting in the shoebox of paid invoices. Everything a tech installs was bought on a ticket with a job name on it, so the truth is already in two systems that have never been compared. This is the freight-audit and telecom-audit model, and no one has brought it to the trades because the people who feel the pain are too busy running trucks to build it.
first_30_days: Offer a free 90-day audit to 10 shop owners from a peer group (a PHCC chapter, Nexstar or Service Roundtable style mastermind). Have them forward statements and give a one-time export. Turn each audit around in 48 hours with a single 'found money' number and a list of specific invoices. Convert the shops with the largest number to the contingency contract. A spreadsheet plus an LLM parsing script is enough for the first ten.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: ServiceTitan Accounts Payable (bill inbox, 3-way matching, Manage Statements, Manage Credits, discrepancy flags), Kojo, BuildOps (Procurement and Payables), Fergus. White space: Nobody I found offers a contingency-fee, done-for-you recovery audit for trade shops. What remains unserved is the customer-side leak: parts on a supply-house ticket with a job name, or pulled from truck stock, that never reached the customer invoice, plus supplier price drift and quoted-price violations tied back to the shop's own pricebook and markup targets. Existing tools (ServiceTitan AP, Kojo, BuildOps, Ramp) are software the shop must adopt and operate, and they focus on paying suppliers correctly. Three parts are open: (1) shops on Housecall Pro, Jobber, FieldEdge or Simpro, or ServiceTitan shops not using Procurement/AP, who have no PO-to-job workflow; (2) the done-for-you, no-recovery-no-fee commercial model, which no software vendor offers; (3) a cross-shop SKU price benchmark from pooled supply-house invoices. I found no evidence anyone has assembled that for residential and light-commercial trade shops. ServiceTitan's Manage Statements and Manage Credits are the closest overlap with the returns-credit and price-error pieces.

title: Fees-in-Kind: Harvest Becomes School Fee Credit
one_liner: A weigh-in and ledger service that lets parents pay school fees with maize, beans and potatoes at a transparent price, while schools get cheaper, steadier food supply.
customer: Boards of management, principals and bursars of public boarding and day secondary schools, including the new senior-school cohorts, plus rural private schools. The end users are smallholder parents in maize, bean and potato zones.
problem: Farm households are asset-rich and cash-poor exactly when fees fall due in January, May and August. Schools already accept 'a tin of maize' informally, but the value is whatever the storekeeper or bursar decides, with no receipts. Meanwhile the same schools buy food through brokers at inflated tender prices, and government capitation often arrives late. Children still get sent home over arrears even when the parents' store is full of grain. Food is often the largest line in a boarding school's budget.
solution: A Fee Credit Ledger. Farmers deliver graded produce to the school store or a village collection point. A standard weigh ticket (photo of the scale plus a moisture reading) generates an SMS receipt, and the value is credited to the learner's fee account at a published reference price such as NCPB or the county market average, minus a small handling margin. The school gets a weekly reconciliation. On the buying side, the platform, registered as an AGPO-eligible youth or women group (check how each school's procurement committee applies the 30% reservation), bids for school food supply and sources from the same parents. It pools, grades and quality-checks (moisture, aflatoxin spot test). An add-on is hermetic storage bags on credit so parents can deliver later in the term rather than dumping at harvest.
why_now: The first CBC cohort entered senior school in January 2026, expanding boarding and food demand, and the next cohort arrives in January 2027, so schools are planning Term 1 supply now. Capitation delays keep squeezing school food budgets. Cheap Bluetooth scales, moisture meters and M-Pesa and SMS receipts make a trustworthy weigh ticket trivial. Principals in Kenya talk in tight associations, so one working pilot spreads fast.
revenue_model: A 4-8% handling margin on food flow: schools pay below their current broker-inclusive price and farmers receive above the broker price. Later a per-learner per-term ledger fee (about KES 50-100). Once the ledger produces credit-quality data, short-term financing of fee arrears or school receivables.
non_obvious_insight: In every rural ward the school is the largest, most predictable institutional food buyer, and the 'fee arrears list' is a timing and valuation mismatch, not poverty. Fintechs treat barter as embarrassing or informal, but for smallholders paying in maize is the default. What is missing is fair valuation and a ledger everyone trusts. The AGPO set-aside is an under-used entry ticket for farmer groups into school tenders.
first_30_days: Sign 2-3 principals through your own old high school or a heads' association branch meeting for a one-term pilot in January 2027. Buy two Bluetooth hanging scales and moisture meters (a few hundred dollars), run the ledger on Google Sheets plus Africa's Talking SMS, and recruit 100 parent households at PTA meetings. Set the price at the midpoint between the farmgate broker price and the school tender price. Register the entity for AGPO and open a supplier profile with the school.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Maziwa ni School Fees (Uasin Gishu County + Space AI + Tuiyo Farmers Cooperative), Food4Education (Tap2Eat), Zeraki (Zeraki Finance), SchoolPay (Uganda, Kenya, Zambia). White space: Nobody I found offers a grain, bean or potato fee-credit ledger for schools. Google News, site fetches and GitHub search turned up no startup, cooperative product or open-source tool that gives standard weigh tickets, SMS receipts and a published reference price. The practice is real but informal, and it is ripe for a trust layer.

Unserved specifics:
(1) Secondary boarding and senior schools in maize, bean and potato zones. Uasin Gishu has taken dairy, and Food4Education owns primary school meals.
(2) Fair valuation and receipts for staples. Principal Kegoro at Nyabisia Secondary (Kisii) says 'we accept them to bring maize or beans, then we value them and receipt them', which is exactly the informal, discretionary step to standardise.
(3) A per-school reconciliation of in-kind credit against arrears lists. Zeraki Finance and SchoolPay show no in-kind receipt type.
(4) Linking fee credit to the school's own kitchen demand, so the grain never needs to be sold on.

Risks that shrink the white space:
(a) The supply-side tender and AGPO piece is weak. IDRC reports only 1-2% of AGPO opportunities reach women, youth and disability-owned firms, with 90-day-plus payment delays and kickback demands. Schools buy 65% from brokers by manual tender.
(b) 2026 is a maize shortage year. The deficit is about 5.4M bags, flour is at KES 153-163 per 2kg, and 53% of smallholders cite lack of surplus. Farmers may hold grain back, and valuation disputes will be sharp.
(c) Tickets for day schools are small. The proposed day-school fee is KES 7,675, against KES 53k-88k for boarding.
(d) One entity being fee-credit collector and tender supplier to the same school invites a conflict-of-interest problem.
(e) Storekeepers and brokers benefit from the current opacity.
(f) Absence from news is not proof of absence. WebSearch was exhausted and Crunchbase and Product Hunt were blocked, so a stealth or very small pilot cannot be ruled out.

title: Insurable-at-Closing: Pay-on-Closing Insurability Sheets for WUI Listings
one_liner: Listing agents order a 48-hour parcel evidence and carrier-routing sheet before a wildfire-zone home goes to market, and the seller pays a flat fee at closing only if the sale closes.
customer: Listing agents and brokerages selling wildland-urban-interface homes in Front Range and mountain markets such as the Boulder foothills, Evergreen and Conifer, Estes Park, Black Forest and the Colorado Springs foothills. Title and escrow officers are the channel, and the seller pays through the settlement statement. A licensed WUI-specialist independent agency is the placement partner.
problem: A lender will not close without a bound homeowners policy. In WUI sales the bind often fails late: the buyer's quote is declined on a score cutoff and the contract clock is running. Neither the seller's nor the buyer's agent can say in advance which carriers will write the lot. No statute helps at that point, because the new-business decline is not a nonrenewal appeal. Free homeowner appeal kits do not touch this moment.
solution: When the home is listed, the agent orders an Insurability Sheet. It is a one-page PDF and a data file with a lot condition ledger from dated imagery and lidar, a ranked list of pre-closing fixes with cost and time to complete, and a carrier route showing which carriers' models see this lot accurately and have a human exception path. The partner agency supplies indicative appetite and quotes. At contract, buyers' agents can re-run the sheet in 24 hours. The lot evidence goes to underwriters as an exception referral at carriers that read it, and away from carriers using coarse 30 m models that will decline the same lot on a raster.
why_now: Colorado WUI homeowners' rates roughly doubled in 2020-2025 (per the parent research) and carriers keep retreating, so insurance availability is now a closing risk. HB25-1182 disclosures mean sellers can now hold a score but not a plan. Cheap high-resolution archives make a 48-hour turnaround affordable. I could not verify local closing-fall-through statistics or new pre-listing tools in this pass, so check both first.
revenue_model: A $395 flat fee on the settlement statement, due only if the sale closes; $150 upfront if the agent prefers. A $75 rapid re-run for buyer-side agents. A placement technology fee or revenue share from the partner agency on policies bound (about 10-15% commission on roughly $5k premiums, renewing yearly), structured with counsel around RESPA and producer-compensation rules. At 8% of roughly 6,000 annual WUI sales in the five focus counties, that is about $0.2M in fees in year one. Expanding across the Western WUI markets lifts this to the low tens of millions.
non_obvious_insight: The same lot gets very different treatment from different carriers. The parent research cites identical Class A homes receiving discounts of 0.7%, 12% and 41%. That suggests the profitable move is routing the lot to the carrier whose model sees it correctly, and not rebutting a score. Routing needs no statutory appeal right, so it works in California, Oregon and Washington where the Colorado law does not apply. The moat is a bindability database of carrier appetite by parcel features and actual bind outcomes. Score vendors see scores, not who binds, and agents see only their own quotes.
first_30_days: Sign one Front Range WUI-specialist independent agency as the licensed placement partner. Recruit 2 title or escrow offices and 5 listing agents. Run 20 listings with the fee contingent on closing and track policy-bound-before-closing rate, days saved and deals rescued. Get a written RESPA and producer-compensation review before any fee reaches a bank account. Turn the results into one case study for brokerage sales meetings.
lineage: mutation of I1148 ('Parcel-Level Rebuttals to Wildfire Insurance Scores'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: FireRisk.ai (RiskIntel AI), DefensibleHome Wildfire Insurance Survival Kit, Defensible Space Score (AACI Group / Five Bays Insurance Agency), Road Home Exteriors 'insurance-grade verification packets'. White space: Nobody found sells imagery-based, parcel-level, insurer-format rebuttal evidence, and nobody sells an agent or HOA 'scan the whole book for likely score errors' workflow. What exists is (a) free or $99 homeowner letter and template kits with no imagery (FireRisk.ai, DefensibleHome, Defensible Space Score), (b) slow on-site certifications (IBHS Wildfire Prepared Home, Wildfire Partners), (c) contractor evidence packets sold with hardening jobs (Road Home Exteriors), and (d) carrier-side imagery scoring (Zesty, Nearmap/Betterview, Cape, Cotality, Verisk) with at most a compliance 'framework' for appeals. Specific unserved wedge: multi-date 15-50 cm imagery that shows a lot's actual condition (irrigated, gravel-scaped, recently cleared) against a 30 m coarse-layer score, formatted for Colorado's 10-day acknowledgement and 30-day decision clock, delivered to independent agents who carry many clients. Genuine caveats that shrink the gap: (1) The premise for California looks broken. AB 75's status page shows it 'held under submission' in Appropriations on 08/29/2025 and no source found shows it enacted (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260AB75). The CA DOI's own report reportedly says there is no formal appeal process. So the 'statutory appeal right' in CA is unverified and Colorado is the only confirmed regime. (2) Colorado HB25-1182 (signed 28 May 2025, effective 1 July 2026, https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/hb25-1182) requires disclosure of the score, range and a plain-language explanation of features. It does not clearly require raw model inputs (fuel class, vegetation density), and it does not require insurers to accept third-party imagery. The 'pull the disclosed model inputs' step may be thin, and DOI enforcement is only that the Commissioner may request a copy of a denied appeal. (3) Insurers can satisfy the law with a manual mitigation discount, so a score correction may not change the premium. (4) Free and $99 substitutes cap willingness to pay for $149-299 per file. (5) Zesty, Nearmap and Cotality hold the same imagery and the carrier relationships, so the durable moat is the concession database, not the imagery. | How this version avoids them: FireRisk.ai, DefensibleHome and the Defensible Space Score serve homeowners disputing an existing score and have nothing for the sale moment or for carrier routing. IBHS and Wildfire Partners are on-site programs that take weeks, and they do not fit a 30-day contract, though they could later validate a sheet. Road Home Exteriors sells evidence with hardening jobs, not before a sale. Zesty, Nearmap, Cape, Cotality and Verisk score for carriers and do not see the buyer's bind attempt. Possible new rivals are quote-at-offer tools and portals with climate scores; they quote from their own models with no lot evidence and no multi-carrier routing. I could not check for those in this pass.

title: Contingency Recovery of Missed Rotable Repair Warranties
one_liner: A success-fee auditor that finds repaired aircraft components that failed inside the shop's warranty window, and turns them into filed claims and cash.
customer: Small and mid-size operators with their own stores and a thin materials team. That means regional airlines, Part 135 cargo feeders and air-ambulance fleets, and Part 145 shops that buy their own exchange units. They pay 20-25% of whatever cash or credit is recovered, and nothing up front.
problem: A repaired starter-generator, bleed valve, hydraulic pump or fuel control that fails 4 months after the shop visit is often covered by warranty. Almost nobody claims it. The tech pulling the unit at 3 AM is trying to make a 6 AM departure and never sees the warranty terms. The repair invoice sits in accounts payable as a PDF. The removal record sits in the maintenance system, and hours and cycles sit in a third place. One materials coordinator owns thousands of removals a year, with 30-90 day claim windows. Three other leaks go unclaimed as well: 'no fault found' evaluation fees on units that were still under warranty, unreturned exchange cores that turn into penalty charges, and repair turnaround-time guarantees that shops never credit because nobody compares PO date to receipt date.
solution: Ingest three exports: removals and installs, PO and repair invoices (PDFs read with an LLM extractor), and the negotiated warranty terms. Match by part number and serial number, including interchangeable P/Ns. Flag every in-warranty failure, late repair turn, disputable NFF fee and open core. Then draft the claim on each vendor's own template, track it to a paid credit, and re-run monthly. Add a 3 AM 'is this unit under warranty?' lookup for maintenance control, so the claim gets started at the moment of removal.
why_now: Airline cost pressure on regionals is high, and mechanic wages rose sharply in 2024-2026, so labor cost per removal is up. Materials teams are being cut while fleets stay old. LLM invoice and PDF extraction only became reliable and cheap enough in the last 18 months, and that is the missing link, because the money sits in unstructured AP documents that MRO software never reads.
revenue_model: Contingency fee of 20-25% of recovered cash and credits, with a 12-month tail on the audit. Later add a $2-5k per month SaaS tier for continuous monitoring, and sell benchmark data on shop warranty behavior to airline procurement teams.
non_obvious_insight: The leak is not in the maintenance system, it is in accounts payable. The tech who removes the part, the coordinator who could file the claim and the department that paid the invoice never share a screen. MRO software vendors will not fix it because warranty terms live in negotiated PDFs, not fields. Repair shops know most eligible claims are never filed, and they price that into their rates. A contingency auditor is the same playbook as freight-audit and telecom-audit firms, aimed at a niche nobody has covered.
first_30_days: Pitch 10 directors of maintenance and materials managers at small regionals, cargo feeders and helicopter EMS operators. Offer a free 12-month leakage audit, and ask them for the three exports. Build the matcher in Python plus an LLM invoice parser, and use a retired warranty or materials coordinator as a paid advisor for vendor quirks. Deliver a ranked claim list to the first 2-3 customers, file the claims yourself, and sign the success-fee agreement on the first credit memo. Publish the aggregate audit finding, such as the percentage of eligible failures that were never claimed, as the lead magnet.

competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Ramco Aviation (MRO/ERP software, warranty management module). White space: Caveat: this verdict rests on thin evidence. The WebSearch budget was exhausted (200 of 200) after the first two lookups. Every further search was refused, and I did not work around that limit. I could only fetch vendor homepages directly. I found no dedicated contingency-fee warranty auditor for rotable repair claims. I also could not rule one out, because I could not run Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or 'startup + key terms' searches. Vendor pages I checked (Trax eMRO, Veryon/Rusada, Pentagon 2000, CAMP) showed no warranty-claims features on their homepages, but homepage silence is weak evidence. I could not check IFS Maintenix (HTTP 429). Gaps that look unserved: (1) an outsourced, success-fee service that reads unstructured repair-invoice PDFs and joins them to removal records. This is the cross-system join the idea describes. (2) Small and mid-size operators such as regionals, Part 135 fleets and air-ambulance operators, which sit below the large ERP buyers Ramco targets. (3) The adjacent leaks, meaning no-fault-found fees within warranty, unreturned core penalties and turnaround-time guarantee credits. None of the vendor pages I read mention these. Unverified risks from my own domain knowledge, not from research: power-by-the-hour and maintenance-service-plan contracts remove warranty exposure for many small fleets. Shop warranty terms are often short and carry exclusions. Getting AP and maintenance-system exports from a small operator is hard. The addressable market may be small. Someone should check all of these before building.

title: Big-Meter Replacement Fund, Repaid by Verified Uplift
one_liner: A meter-brand-neutral fund buys, installs and owns a utility's worst large meters at zero upfront cost. The utility repays 70% of measured incremental revenue for up to 5 years, with an open verification protocol that makes it an underwritable asset class.
customer: Utilities with 5k-100k connections that know their big meters are old but have no capex or staff. That is most utilities carrying PFAS and lead-line programs. The wedge buyer is a city or district finance director who can sign a no-cost, contingent-payment services contract under their small-purchase limit. Later, infrastructure lenders and the SRF or muni-lease programs that co-finance the fund.
problem: Replacing a large meter is a financing problem, not an information problem. A top-quartile large meter (3-10 inch) costs about $5-25k installed and can recover $6-15k a year in missed water and sewer revenue, which is a payback of about 1-2 years. Yet it stays unfunded. The benefit lands in the revenue line that nobody budgets as upside, while the cost hits scarce capex competing with lead lines and PFAS treatment. Council needs a procurement, an appropriation and a crew. An audit like the sharpened version tells them what to fix, but leaves them to fund and execute it. ESCOs bundle it into large projects with the vendor's own hardware, and meter vendors finance only their own meters.
solution: Underwrite: the screen ranks candidate meters by expected uplift and only meters with payback under about 2 years enter the fund. Verify: an open measurement and verification protocol (pre-swap on-site accuracy test at three flow rates, post-swap test, then 12 months of billing versus matched peer accounts) in the style of IPMVP for energy. Fund: the fund buys meters through distributors at volume and pays independent plumbers and a test subcontractor for the swap. Repay: the utility pays a metering-service fee of 70% of verified incremental revenue per meter, for up to 60 months or until 1.8x of capital is returned, never more, then owns the meter. Payments are contingent, not debt, and recovery is prospective, so no back-billing. Every swap adds a before-and-after label to the yield model, which lowers the cost of capital. Later, pool contracts and sell them to infrastructure debt or bank warehouse lines.
why_now: Revenue-backed, measured-savings financing has already worked for solar PPAs and energy performance contracts once a standard M&V existed. Water meters have none. Utilities are capital-starved by PFAS and lead-line mandates and need off-balance-sheet fixes. AMI interval data makes before-and-after verification cheap enough to sell to lenders. Data engineering means a small team can build the underwriting model, and distributors are eager to move meter volume.
revenue_model: Return on deployed capital: assumed 25-30% net unlevered (about $9k average installed cost, about $6k a year of measured uplift, 70% share, 2-2.5x lifetime multiple, less yield and dispute losses). Fees: 3-5% origination and a verification fee per meter. Later: a warehouse line then securitization of the contract pool. Data licensing of the accuracy-by-model-and-age dataset to lenders, consultants and vendors. Start-up capital: a $250-400k first pilot from angels or a revenue-based lender, plus extended payment terms from a meter distributor.
non_obvious_insight: An accurate large meter is a small, measurable cash-producing asset with almost no credit risk, because its yield, not the city's credit, pays it back. What is missing is a trusted way to measure the yield. Whoever writes and owns the verification protocol and holds the labeled before-and-after data has a standard-setter's position and a compounding cost-of-capital advantage: each verified swap makes the next loan cheaper. Meter distributors are suppliers and floor-plan lenders here, not enemies, because the fund is a volume buyer that creates demand they cannot create.
first_30_days: Write v0.1 of the verification protocol as a 2-page public document and get two reviewers: a water-loss practitioner and a municipal attorney (to review the contingent service-contract form and the state's non-appropriation rules). Get 90-180 day terms from two distributors on 25 large meters and a rate for a test-rig subcontractor. Run free top-100 scans for 6 utilities of 10-40k connections and pick the one with the best yield and a cooperative finance director. Propose a no-cost 25-meter pilot with 70% of verified uplift for 60 months. Line up the first $250-400k. Aim to have the pilot contract on a council agenda inside 90 days.
