title: Smoke Report Autopsy for Policyholder Advocates
one_liner: An adequacy auditor that scores any carrier-side smoke, ash and soot report against a public, versioned sampling grid. It then drafts the AB 1795 deficiency letter and supplemental sampling plan, and sells to public adjusters and plaintiff attorneys in the Eaton and Palisades zones.
customer: Wedge: 15-25 licensed public adjuster firms working standing-home smoke claims in Altadena, Pasadena, Pacific Palisades and Malibu, plus 3-5 plaintiff firms running the Ghazarian-style class actions against carrier-retained hygiene vendors. Later: homeowners buying direct at about $295, then carrier claims-legal teams running pre-flight audits on their own vendors.
problem: Every standing-home claimant holds a carrier-vendor IH report saying 'clean' or 'minor'. Neither the public adjuster nor the attorney can tell quickly whether it was under-sampled. Carrier-retained hygienists reportedly take about 10 samples in 3,000 sq ft, skip attics, wall cavities and HVAC, and compare results to urban background dust. A CIH second opinion costs $2k-$4k+ and takes weeks from a scarce pool. Purdue's free review is capacity-limited and does not produce claim-ready output. From Jan 1, 2027 AB 1795 makes insurers pay for testing that is 'necessary', but only if someone shows what is necessary and missing.
solution: Upload the IH report and lab PDF. LLM extraction with human QA pulls sample count, locations, media (wipe, tape lift, air, bulk), comparison basis, detection limits and skipped zones. It scores them against a public 'Adequacy Grid' built from AIHA's wildfire guide, IICRC/RIA/CIRI, 40 CFR 745.227 and 8 CCR 1529, with every criterion cited. Within 48 hours the customer gets a 2-page scorecard listing what was not sampled, a statute-cited deficiency letter for the PA or attorney to send, and a supplemental sampling plan that a partner CIH-of-record can sign, with a priced quote from a partner testing firm. The plaintiff tier ingests hundreds of reports in batch for pattern analytics (share with zero attic samples, samples per 1,000 sq ft by vendor). The grid is versioned so it re-maps when DTSC publishes standards in 2028-29. We do not sample, employ technicians, or give expert opinions.
why_now: AB 1795 was signed 9/15/2026 and takes effect 1/1/2027. It creates a 30-day inspection duty and a duty to pay for necessary testing, and it presumes smoke, ash and soot in a standing home came from the fire. Class actions over vendor sampling were filed in Feb 2026, LA County sued State Farm on 8/31/2026, and 13,000+ standing homes with smoke damage are in play. Cheap LLM document extraction makes a 48-hour, hundreds-of-dollars audit feasible where it used to be a $3k CIH engagement.
revenue_model: Public adjusters pay $395 per audit, or $2,500 a month for up to 10 active files. The CIH-signed supplemental sampling plan costs $900, split 50/50 with the partner CIH. Plaintiff-firm pattern analytics run $40k-$150k per engagement, for example a 300-report batch. The partner testing firm pays a flat referral fee on supplemental sampling it wins, or we take none if that raises fee-splitting concerns. Phase 2 sells carrier claims-legal teams a $2k-$5k per-vendor-report pre-flight audit. Bottom-up: even 15% of 13,000 homes at $395 plus a few analytics contracts is about $1.5M-$2.5M in year one, so the wedge is small and the dataset is the asset.
non_obvious_insight: The unit of leverage is the omission list, not the test result. AB 1795 obliges the insurer to pay for necessary testing, and a scored list of what was not sampled and why it matters converts a fuzzy fight into a checklist the adjuster must answer in writing. Every audit also writes one structured row (vendor, square footage, samples, comparator, zones skipped), so the tool quietly builds the largest labeled dataset of how carrier vendors sample. Counter-positioning is real: HygieneTech, Rimkus and Safeguard cannot sell a tool that indicts carrier-side sampling without alienating their own clients.
first_30_days: Week 1: collect 25 real IH reports with consent from EFRU volunteers, two public adjusters and one attorney. Sign two CIHs at about $150/hr to review the rubric, and a toxicologist as advisor. Weeks 2-3: build Grid v0.1 as a spreadsheet plus extraction pipeline, targeting over 90% field-level accuracy on the 25 reports. Run free 48-hour audits for 10 PA files. Track whether the deficiency letter gets the carrier or FAIR Plan to authorize additional testing. Week 4: start charging $395 from audit #11, aiming for 30 paid audits and one attorney LOI for a 100-report batch pilot at about $25k. Before day 15, confirm from the chaptered AB 1795 text that there is no qualified-person or licensure rule that blocks a non-CIH from drafting a sampling plan for CIH signature.
lineage: mutation of I0715 ('Interim Smoke-Damage Protocol Before the State Standard'), type: sharpened
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Hygiene Technologies International (HygieneTech), Rimkus, Safeguard EnviroGroup (Brad Kovar), EHS Analytical Solutions. White space: Mostly assessment supply and free guidance are crowded, so the raw 'do smoke testing' and 'publish a protocol' layers are not white space. Dozens of CIH-led firms sell $2k-$4k+ assessments and clearance certificates. AIHA, IICRC/RIA/CIRI, Purdue and EFRU already publish free or cheap protocols. Safeguard EnviroGroup is already pitching a 'defensible framework' to carriers. State agencies (AB 1795 drafts) planned to certify IHs, contractors and labs, which undercuts the training-fee line.

Still unserved: (1) Carrier and TPA operations under AB 1795. Nobody offers a claim-level compliance layer with the 30-day inspection clock, an audit-ready sampling plan mapped to zones, chain-of-custody records and an evidence file, sold as software. Carriers are 'technically opposed' but must comply from 1/1/2027, and CAT surge capacity is the pain. (2) Sampling-design defensibility. The fight is over how many samples, where, and against what background, and no independent tool scores a sampling plan or existing IH report for adequacy, though this is what class actions and the Purdue review turn on. (3) A neutral, versioned crosswalk from AIHA/IICRC/40 CFR 745.227 lead-dust levels and 8 CCR 1529 asbestos to a per-home plan, which updates when DTSC issues standards in 2028-29. (4) Pooled, structured sampling data across claims, which is what regulators reuse. EFRU holds only a few dozen homes.

Two facts weaken the 'vacuum' framing. Interim lead and asbestos thresholds already exist in AB 1642 (40 CFR 745.227(e)(8)(viii) and 8 CCR 1529). The vacuum is mainly sampling design and non-lead contaminants such as cyanide, other metals and dioxins.

Structural risks: the buyer conflict, because carriers may not adopt a protocol seen as policyholder-friendly and policyholder-side buyers want a testifying CIH rather than software. Remote IH sign-off and technician-collected samples may run into CIH and certification expectations. Any advantage is capped at the moment DTSC publishes standards.

Research limits: my web-search budget ran out before I could run Crunchbase, YC and TechCrunch-specific queries. The general startup searches (wildfire smoke assessment startup, chain-of-custody kits, technician network) found only wildfire-detection companies (Pano AI, FireScan, FireSafe AI), none in post-fire smoke-damage assessment. Treat 'no funded startup' as probable, not proven. | How this version avoids them: HygieneTech, Rimkus, Safeguard EnviroGroup, EHS Analytical, Home BioTesting and Vert-type shops all sell sampling supply and are either carrier-conflicted or capacity-bound. We sell no sampling, so EHS and Home BioTesting become the partners who fulfil the supplemental plans and gain lead flow. Purdue's free review is bounded by grad-student capacity and has no claim-language deliverable, SLA or batch mode; we cite its method and offer a data-share and donation instead of competing. IICRC, AIHA and EFRU publish guidance and maps but sell no per-claim operational tool, so we build on them and ask EFRU for a data partnership. Safeguard's 'defensible framework' is a carrier-side essay, whereas ours is a scoring engine aimed at the policyholder side. State standards in 2028-29 change the grid's contents but not the need for an audit tool, so the business survives the standard rather than dying with it.

title: Warranty Clock Recovery Audits for Idle Halls
one_liner: A contingency-fee service that finds and files the warranty claims on energized-but-empty data halls before OEM warranty clocks silently expire.
customer: Colocation developers, powered-shell landlords, neocloud operators and enterprise owners with phased or delayed-tenant builds, especially those with halls commissioned 6-14 months ago and not yet loaded. The owner pays a percentage of recovered value, plus an optional per-asset tracking subscription.
problem: Warranty clocks on generators, UPS systems, chillers, CRAH/CDUs, switchgear, and batteries usually start at shipment or startup, not when a tenant loads the hall. With delayed leases and mid-build AI redesigns, halls sit energized and idle for months. Many defects only show under real load (UPS capacitors, chiller compressors, wet-stacking gensets, breaker trip curves, coolant chemistry). By the time the tenant ramps, the warranty has expired. The turnover package is 50,000+ pages of PDFs that ops never reads, the punch-list deferrals are lost, and OEM maintenance records required to keep coverage valid are often missing. Nobody owns the clock.
solution: Ingest POs, OEM warranty terms, startup sheets, Cx reports, shipping documents and maintenance logs with an LLM pipeline to build a serial-number-level warranty ledger with real expiry dates and voiding conditions. Flag anything expiring within 120 days. Run a targeted load-dependent-defect inspection before expiry (thermography, oil and coolant samples, capacitor and battery checks, breaker testing). File claims, negotiate warranty start-date deferrals or extensions with the OEM while leverage still exists, and fix missing maintenance-record gaps. For new builds, sell a PO-stage clause pack that defers warranty start to beneficial occupancy.
why_now: There is a glut of speculative shells and delayed tenant handoffs. Reporting in 2026 shows close to half of planned US builds slipping, with only about a third of 2026 target capacity under active construction. That means many halls are powered, commissioned and idle. Equipment was bought at peak prices with tariffs on steel, aluminum and copper, so each lapsed warranty is worth more. LLMs can now read messy closeout binders cheaply, which was the labor bottleneck for audits like this.
revenue_model: 25-30% of recovered value or avoided cost on claims and negotiated extensions, no fee if nothing is recovered. Optional $150-400 per asset per year tracking subscription. $15K-40K fixed-fee closeout audits for owners who want certainty. PO-stage clause-pack consulting for developers.
non_obvious_insight: The warranty is the only major asset on a data center balance sheet that expires silently. OEMs will defer warranty start dates at PO time, but almost no one negotiates it because the project team is fighting for delivery slots, not paperwork. After the fact, the owner's ops team inherits the docs with no idea when the clocks started. The money is in the punch-list items that were 'to be fixed later' and the load-dependent defects that only appear after the hall is finally used.
first_30_days: Find 3 owner-operators through PM and Cx network contacts with halls energized 8-11 months ago and not fully loaded. Offer a free 10-day scan of their closeout binders in exchange for a contingency agreement on any claims. Build the extraction pipeline on real binders (gensets, UPS, chillers first). Deliver a 'expiring within 90 days' hit list and file the first claims before the first invoice.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Ethyco (data center commissioning, warranty-phase support), Anyset AI (agentic closeout / warranty tracking), Nomic (AEC document AI, closeout), Trane delayed start-up warranty (OEM rider). White space: Nobody I found combines all of these for data center MEP: (1) a serial-number-level clock ledger built for idle or deferred-start halls, (2) a pre-expiry loaded stress test using the idle capacity, (3) OEM claim filing and start-date deferral negotiation, and (4) success-fee or fixed-fee pricing sold to the owner or its lender. The pieces exist separately. Anyset and Nomic do doc extraction. Ethyco-style Cx firms do a 10-month warranty review. Wind and solar have end-of-warranty inspection and claims firms. OEMs sell delayed-start riders. Load-bank vendors have the hardware. Data center power and cooling MEP has no dedicated end-of-warranty claims specialist that I could find. Three structural weaknesses limit the wedge. (a) The clocks mostly start at OEM startup, and startup plus IST with load banks already loads equipment in Cx, so the 'idle for 12+ months' exposure is narrower than the pitch implies. It mainly hits gear started early or shipped more than 18 months before use. (b) 'Recovered value' is really avoided repair cost. It is hard to measure and easy for OEMs to dispute, and OEMs can deny on storage or light-load grounds (wet stacking is explicitly excluded, https://cliffordpower.com/wet-stacking-why-its-important-to-load-bank-your-diesel-generator/). A pure 25-30% contingency model will be hard to collect. (c) Documents are the commodity step, so the moat has to be inspection plus OEM leverage, not the LLM pipeline.

title: Independent Answer Key for Synthetic Respondents
one_liner: Invert the referee: a neutral scoring authority that holds fresh, verified-human ground truth, and scores synthetic-respondent and digital-twin vendors against it in quarterly pre-registered, sealed-prediction benchmarks.
customer: Two-sided. Vendors: synthetic-respondent, persona and digital-twin startups and the survey platforms adding synthetic boosts. Buyers: CPG, pharma and financial-services insights and innovation teams and research agencies being pitched 'AI respondents' and unsure whom to believe. Later: AI labs that need uncontaminated human-opinion evals.
problem: Synthetic-respondent vendors claim high accuracy on self-chosen benchmarks. Backtests against old polls leak, because published polls and concept-test norms are in the models' training data, and vendors can cherry-pick questions. Buyers have no neutral way to tell which claim is real before betting a launch decision on it. The parent evidence that agents pass 99.8% of attention checks shows LLM personas mimic humans on surface features, which cuts both ways: it enables fraud and it makes synthetic research plausible. Nobody holds fresh verified-human answers on questions asked after model cutoffs, with the vendor's predictions locked in beforehand.
solution: A predict-then-reveal benchmark. Each quarter, the firm and a buyer advisory board write about 80 novel questions and concepts, including anonymised buyer concept tests under NDA. Vendors submit hash-committed sealed predictions of the answer distributions for named demographic targets. The firm fields the items to 1,000-3,000 verified humans, address-recruited and device-attested, licensed from partners (NORC, Verasight, Prolific or a university survey centre) so no one panel controls the answer key. It scores distribution error, rank-order of concept winners, subgroup fidelity and calibration of stated uncertainty, and publishes a leaderboard. Vendors pay for private diagnostics and for a licence to cite their scored accuracy, never for placement. Buyers pay for full reports and for a 'bake-off as a service', running a shortlist of 3 vendors on 10 of the buyer's own concepts against 400 verified humans. Endgame: the growing library of pre-registered human ground truth becomes shared infrastructure. It calibrates hybrid human-plus-synthetic samples, is licensed to AI labs as fresh opinion evals, and feeds the original bot-audit business off the same panel.
why_now: Synthetic-respondent and digital-twin companies raised large rounds in 2025-26 and are getting enterprise pilots (specific rounds not verified in this session, so check). Model releases every few months make static benchmarks stale and leaky, which turns a benchmark into a recurring re-fielding business. Pew's Aug 2026 study is a public design template for benchmarking against address-recruited samples. Buyers who lived through the panel-fraud scare now ask 'how do you know it is right?' by reflex.
revenue_model: Vendors pay $8-25k per quarterly private diagnostic and $30-100k/yr for an audited accuracy-claim licence. Buyers pay $10-25k/yr for full reports and $20-40k per bake-off. Founding-member pre-sales fund wave 1: 8 buyers at $15k covers a 1,000-human wave. Later, AI-lab dataset licences of $100-500k/yr. Control-panel cost is the main COGS at about $10-40 per verified complete, which suggests 60-70% gross margin once pre-sales cover each wave.
non_obvious_insight: The verified-human panel is worth more as the answer key for AI than as a shield against AI, and the business wins whichever way the synthetic-research bet goes. If synthetic respondents work, everyone needs a scorer and a calibration anchor. If they fail, buyers need proof and a return to human samples. Fraud and progress both raise demand for the reference. The product is not data but a commitment protocol (sealed predictions, then reveal), which solves the training-data leakage that no static dataset can. Refusing to be scored becomes a signal of weakness, which is the flywheel that turns a benchmark into a standard, the way MLPerf-style or leaderboard-style evaluators gained authority.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: write the protocol and scoring spec (sealing method, metrics, no pay-for-placement rule) and publish it openly. Recruit 5 founding buyer-side advisors (CPG or pharma insights heads) at $5k pilot memberships. Days 5-20: invite 6-8 synthetic-respondent vendors to a free founding wave slot in exchange for submitting sealed predictions. Days 15-30: finalize 40 novel questions, hash-commit vendor predictions, and field wave 0 to 600-1,000 verified humans from a partner for roughly $10-20k. Publish the first leaderboard by day 45. Kill test: fewer than 4 vendors willing to submit, or fewer than 3 buyers who say they would pay for the results.
lineage: mutation of I0716 ('Independent Referee for Survey Panel Data'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Data Quality Co-op (DQC), Verasight, Verisoul, CloudResearch (Sentry, Engage, Bot Olympics). White space: Detection is crowded and getting cheap: Verisoul, Roundtable, dtect, CloudResearch, Kantar Qubed, Research Defender, PureScore, ReDem and CleanID all sell it, some at cents per respondent. Cross-supplier scorecards already exist too, since Data Quality Co-op is a neutral clearinghouse. Building a detection ensemble or a generic vendor scorecard would be a fifth-to-tenth entrant against funded players.

What I did not find anyone selling:
1. A per-study ground-truth calibration. This means running a slice of the same questionnaire on a verified, address-recruited human control group and then reporting contamination-adjusted estimates with error bounds. Every vendor I found detects and removes. None quantifies how much bias survives the cleaning, and none re-estimates the result against a known-real reference. Pew's finding that voter-file matching removed valid respondents and made the error worse suggests 'remove the flagged' is itself a source of bias.
2. A neutral buyer-side referee that owns no sample. dtect is neutral but only sells entry-time detection. DQC is neutral but does not audit individual studies or supply a control sample. Verasight owns verified humans but sells sample.
3. Independent, third-party verification of the vendors' own accuracy claims. CloudResearch and Verisoul each claim 100% agent detection from internal or self-run tests. The Bot Olympics is MIT-judged but tests CloudResearch's own system.

The missing piece for a startup is the control panel. Building an address-recruited, device-attested panel of about 2,000 people is slow and expensive. The likelier route is to partner with or license an existing one (Verasight, NORC, Pew or Ipsos-style panels), not recruit from scratch.

This conclusion has limits. My WebSearch budget ran out at 200 calls, so I could not run the Crunchbase, YC or Product Hunt checks or search for a second wave of small startups. I also could not confirm funding for DQC, Roundtable, dtect or Verasight. | How this version avoids them: Every competitor in the parent's research defends human samples against bots (Verisoul, dtect, Roundtable, CloudResearch, Kantar Qubed, PureScore, ReDem) or sells verified sample (Verasight), or writes standards without testing (GDQ). None scores synthetic respondents. CloudResearch's Bot Olympics grades detectors on its own turf and is not neutral. Verasight's replication of Pew shows its own panel is cleaner, so it sells sample and could not be an arbiter between vendors that compete with its product. DQC is neutral but aggregates fraud signals. It does not run sealed-prediction tests against fresh human truth. Pew and NORC could field this, but a non-profit research org will not run a recurring commercial scoring service. Academic synthetic-survey benchmarks exist but are static and leak into training data. I could not verify whether a commercial neutral scorer already exists because the web-search budget ran out, so check before building.

title: Graduate Pay Ledger for CDL Schools and Carriers
one_liner: CDL schools get the verified placement and earnings evidence Workforce Pell requires by having graduates upload settlement stubs to a pay-verification app. Carriers pay to reach those graduates with verified pay pages, and lenders pay for stub-based income packets.
customer: Small and mid-size CDL schools and other short-program providers (paying per completer verified) as the beachhead. Carriers with 50-1,000 trucks that pay $6-15k to hire a driver (verified-pay badge and graduate funnel), mortgage and auto lenders serving drivers, and state workforce boards.
problem: Workforce Pell requires verified placement (about 70%) with a clock that starts before the governor application, and CDL schools typically track completion, not employment. State wage records lag by quarters and miss owner-operators and per-diem pay. Meanwhile the pay-verification app has a cold-start problem: recruiting drivers one Facebook group at a time is slow and noisy.
solution: At completion, schools enroll graduates in the pay app. In exchange for a verified profile and a small incentive, graduates upload their first settlement stubs at 30, 90 and 180 days. The AI extracts employer, paid miles, deadhead, detention and pay per hour away from home. The school gets an audit-ready placement and earnings ledger, the governor application packet, and an earnings-premium exposure score. Carriers that look good buy a Verified Pay page and a graduate applicant funnel, and lenders buy income packets built from stubs.
why_now: Workforce Pell went live for provider approvals in 2026 and the placement and completion evidence rules make this a compliance purchase with a deadline. The stub-parsing AI is cheap now. Carriers are paying up to $15k per driver hired and are locked out of trust because drivers only believe stubs.
revenue_model: $150-300 per completer verified or $4-12k per year per program. $3-5k for a governor application packet. $1.5-3k earnings-premium exposure report. $500-3,000 per month carrier subscriptions for verified pay pages and graduate funnel. $300-1,000 lender referral fees per funded loan. Free for graduates.
non_obvious_insight: A settlement stub proves placement, employer, and earnings in a single document that drivers, carriers and lenders already trust, which employer-email verification and state wage matching can't do for small carriers or per-diem pay. The school-by-carrier pay matrix is a data product in its own right. It tells each school which carriers to steer graduates toward, which raises next year's placement rate and protects Pell eligibility, so verification pays for itself in outcomes.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 CDL schools in two states that have opened Workforce Pell approval, at a $1.5k pilot price. Backfill the last 12 months of completers by text, asking for stubs, to produce a baseline verified placement rate and a sample governor packet. Publish a 'State of Real Pay for New CDL Graduates' report naming carriers. Sell Verified Pay badges to the 3-5 mid-size fleets that hire the most graduates and sign one bank-statement mortgage broker for lender leads.
lineage: hybrid of I0916 + I0227 (Placement Proof for Workforce Pell Providers + Verified Pay Receipts for Truck Driver Hiring). Why stronger: Placement Proof alone has to chase completers by text and email, and the pay app alone has a slow consumer cold start. Combined, schools deliver a captive, motivated cohort of new drivers every month, the pay data comes from the exact graduates schools need to verify, and carriers and lenders subsidize a verification service that schools would otherwise pay for entirely themselves.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Ellucian (incl. former Anthology CampusNexus SIS, Occupation Insight), Populi, Gradelink, Lightcast. White space: Confidence is LOW. My WebSearch budget was exhausted (200 of 200) before any searches ran. Only 9 direct page fetches went through, and they returned homepage-level content. I also tried a Google URL through WebFetch and then stopped, because that was an attempt to get around the search limit. I found no direct competitor, but I did not search for one, so this is not evidence that none exists. Homepage checks of Populi, Ellucian/Anthology, Gradelink and Lightcast showed no Workforce Pell or placement-verification features. Orbund's site was bot-blocked, and the Federal Register and ed.gov pages redirected or returned 403, so I could not check the rule text. Likely unserved wedge: a Workforce Pell-specific product that (1) backfills the 12-month look-back by contacting completers and employers, (2) reconciles evidence to the rule's placement definition, and (3) produces the governor application packet for small CDL, CNA, barbering and cosmetology schools. Not searched, so still unknown: startups or Product Hunt and YC entries; existing placement-verification services already sold to accredited career schools (ACCSC, NACCAS, COE reporting); consultancies selling this as a service; state-built portals; and SIS vendor Workforce Pell roadmaps. Structural risks visible without further research: (a) if the final rule lets states verify placement from UI wage records, a self-collected pay-stub product loses much of its value; (b) SIS vendors can bolt this on as a feature; (c) the number of approved programs, and so the buyer count, may be small at first. || Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: TruckersReport (carrier reviews and salary survey), Best Fleets to Drive For (CarriersEdge), Tenstreet (Driver Pulse, IntelliApp, Hiring Center), Drive My Way. White space: Web search was unavailable (the session's 200-search budget was used up), so this rests on about 25 direct page fetches plus prior knowledge. Confidence is moderate to low. A reviewer should re-run searches for 'verified driver pay', 'settlement stub scanner' and 'trucker mortgage per diem' before committing.

I found no product that does all of this: (1) collect settlement stubs, (2) verify them with fraud checks, and (3) publish per-carrier, receipts-backed effective pay, including dollars per hour away from home. The closest, TruckersReport, has an unverified self-reported salary survey run by a site paid by carriers' recruiting budgets. Best Fleets to Drive For is survey-based. Tenstreet and Drive My Way own recruiting flow but show no pay-verification product.

Specific unserved gaps:
- A trust-backed pay number that uses stubs as proof, computed as dollars per hour on the road rather than per mile.
- Lease-purchase and owner-operator drivers, whose settlements are itemized and who are the most exposed to deceptive ads.
- A stub-based income packet that handles per-diem structures for non-QM and bank-statement lenders. Truv and Argyle verify through payroll connections and are not built for per-diem trucker income.

Weak points that could still sink it:
1. Cold start and selection bias. Unhappy drivers upload more, and carriers with a bad median will not buy a badge. A pay-for-badge model also has a credibility conflict.
2. Stubs do not show time away from home. Hours-away metrics need driver-entered dates or ELD integration, which is hard.
3. The truth-in-leasing itemized-settlement rule (49 CFR 376.12) applies to owner-operator leases, not W-2 company drivers. The idea's 'raw material already exists' claim is only partly true. I could not fetch the regulation this session.
4. Publishing rankings of named carriers invites legal threats. Self-published analytics are not covered by Section 230 the way user reviews are.
5. Per-funded-loan referral fees to a non-lender may run into RESPA Section 8, so this needs counsel. Lenders will also likely re-verify borrower-supplied stubs, which limits the lender product's value. This is from prior knowledge and not verified.

title: Recorder Rails: County-Funded Clean Index of Instruments
one_liner: AI re-indexing and compliance scans that counties buy from their own records-modernization funds. In return we hold the cleaned, entity-resolved index of every non-deed instrument, which becomes the data layer for assembly alerts and much else.
customer: County recorders and clerks (about 3,100 counties), who pay first, starting with mid-size rural and exurban counties in data-center and energy corridors where economic development offices also want the assembly view. Downstream buyers are the parent's developers, utilities and funds, plus ag lenders and title-adjacent firms.
problem: The parent's product depends on county-by-county recorder access and on document types that are often wrong ('Other', 'Miscellaneous', 'Agreement'). Ingestion is a grind, bulk commercial-use rules vary, and the good data is scattered. Counties have their own pains: aging archives, mandated redaction of sensitive data, covenant-review requests and property-fraud pressure, all with thin staff. They already spend on indexing and digitization from earmarked funds. Nobody owns a clean cross-county index of non-deed instruments.
solution:
1. Sell the county a fixed-price Hidden Instruments Audit. AI reclassifies its mislabeled and 'Other' instruments from the images, corrects grantor and grantee indexing, flags sensitive-data and statutory items such as discriminatory covenants, and gives the county a corrected index and an economic-development view of large instruments.
2. In the agreement, the county gives bulk access to the images and index at cost, and we keep the right to publish the derived classification and entity graph. The underlying records are already public.
3. Publish an open taxonomy for non-deed instruments, in the manner of MISMO for mortgages, so counties and vendors can adopt it.
4. Keep the labeled corpus and the LLC-family graph proprietary and build products on it: Courthouse Tape alerts, the utility site-control check, landowner tools, alt-data licences and collateral-encumbrance alerts for ag lenders.
why_now: LLM vision has collapsed the cost of reading a scanned page, so a re-index that once cost a labor-intensive vendor per-page fees is now cheap. Counties are under fresh mandates to review archives: covenant-removal laws in a number of states, and reportedly some large counties have already run AI covenant scans (verify which). Property-fraud concern is high. FinCEN's exemption of domestic companies from beneficial-ownership reporting makes primary-record entity resolution more valuable. The large-load land rush gives the resulting index an immediate paying use. Rural counties facing data center proposals want visibility into assembly.
revenue_model: County audits at $9k-$40k per county, fitted under small-purchase thresholds and paid from records-modernization or technology funds, then $5k-$20k a year to maintain. Data licences to funds at $50k-$150k a year. Downstream product revenue per the parent: developer or utility seats at $2k-$8k a month and title packets at $750-$2,000. A plausible year-three target is 300 counties at about $25k, or $7.5M, plus $5M-$10M of licences and subscriptions. Gross margin on data products should exceed 70% once ingestion is standardized.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource is county cooperation, not the classifier. So invert who pays. Instead of buying access from counties, we get paid by them to solve a problem they already fund, and the by-product is the corpus. A county that gets a corrected index and a free economic-development dashboard has little reason to block a downstream data feed, and other counties will copy the arrangement. This is a cornered resource plus switching costs that build county by county. Incumbents face asymmetry: indexing and digitization vendors earn from labor-based per-page work, so AI re-indexing at a fraction of the price undercuts their own revenue. Title plants index for title, not for cross-county assembly detection.
first_30_days: Run an offline proof on two rumored-project counties. Pull 24 months of instruments, reclassify 'Other' and 'Agreement' filings, and count how many option memoranda were recorded before the announcement. If that count is low, shift the wedge to easement and transmission detection. Show each recorder the result: 'We found N large instruments mislabeled as Other.' Offer a $9,500 audit to three counties, and separately sell the free 'who is assembling where' memo to 10 site-selection consultants to fund the corpus. Check each state's rules on commercial use of bulk records and on data-sharing agreements, and get county counsel comfortable.
lineage: mutation of I0773 ('Courthouse Tape: Land-Assembly Radar for Infrastructure'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: ATTOM Data, Reonomy, Regrid, Enverus. White space: The specific product in the idea, a feed that reads recorded option memoranda, leases and easements from county recorders, classifies them from the image rather than the clerk's label, clusters LLC families by notary, return-to firm and address, and alerts on assembly patterns, was not found at any vendor I could read. Everything I could read is adjacent. Parcel and ownership vendors (Regrid, ATTOM, Reonomy) sell deeds, mortgages and LLC piercing but not options or easements. Siting and diligence vendors (Paces, Enverus, GridCARE) help a client find its own site. Project trackers (Cleanview, DC Byte, Heatmap Pro, Data Center Watch) start at permit or public news. Land-management vendors (Pandell, Enverus LandScape) manage a client's own documents. What remains open is cross-county, image-level reading of recorded non-deed instruments to detect other parties' assembly, sold as alerts. It is plausibly protected by the hard part, which is getting recorder access county by county, not the ML. The main structural doubts I could not test are whether developers actually record option memoranda before announcement, and how many counties allow bulk commercial pulls of document images. | How this version avoids them: The parent's competitors are adjacent data sellers: ATTOM, Regrid and Reonomy sell deeds, mortgages and parcels; Enverus, Paces and GridCARE serve a client's own site; Cleanview, DC Byte and Heatmap Pro start after permits or news; Pandell manages a client's own documents. None of them controls the recorder relationship. Title plants such as First American DataTree hold indexed documents for title workflows, not a cleaned cross-county alert feed. The county-software and digitization vendors (Tyler, Fidlar and Kofile appear to be the main ones, none verified here) are the real risk and might build the same thing. We differ by working on top of whichever system the county runs, by contracting with the county rather than the vendor, and by owning the entity graph. Enverus can add a feature but not a hundred county contracts.

title: Same-Week MFP Refunds for Senior-Care Pharmacies
one_liner: A refund-purchase facility for independent long-term-care pharmacies that becomes the payee of record on Medicare's negotiated-price refunds and pays out within two business days, underwritten claim by claim.
customer: Owners and CFOs of independent closed-door long-term-care (LTC) and senior-living pharmacies, and groups of 3-30 of them. First reached through the Senior Care Pharmacy Coalition, whose members warned that 60% may close in 2026 without a fix. Our estimate, to be checked against real claims exports, is a float of $150k to $1M+ per LTC pharmacy (Eliquis, Xarelto, Jardiance, Januvia, Farxiga and Entresto dominate senior volume). That is 5-30x the $27k a month NCPA cites for an average community pharmacy, so each logo is worth far more.
problem: LTC pharmacies pay wholesalers full price on a 7-14 day cycle and then wait about 21 days (CMS/MTF average; 67% of NCPA respondents wait 22+ days) for the difference between price and Maximum Fair Price. They already carry slow nursing-home and PBM receivables. Their bank has a blanket lien and almost certainly treats a non-trade manufacturer refund as ineligible collateral, so the refund float is funded from owner savings or by cutting stock of the drugs seniors need. Merchant cash advances cost far too much for a stream that is statutory.
solution: 1) Onboard with 8-12 weeks of PMS claims exports and MTF remittance files. The free 'refund aging and dilution audit' is our underwriting diligence, not the product. 2) Make the refund land where we control it. Preferred route is being the pharmacy's designated payee, either as a registered third-party support entity if CMS and the facilitator allow it, or through a deposit account under a control agreement. That puts cash upstream of the wholesaler's weekly debit. Fallback is use-of-proceeds control, where the advance pays the MFP-drug invoice lines straight to the wholesaler. 3) Each week, score every MFP claim for dilution and buy the scored-eligible refunds at about 85% within two business days. The 15% reserve, net of our fee, is released when the actual MTF payment arrives. Recourse is limited to dilution through the reserve. There is no blanket credit recourse, and no 'non-recourse' promise we cannot keep. 4) Get the existing senior lender's consent or carve-out at onboarding, pitched as relief for their borrower's cash squeeze. Capital starts at $500k-$2M from a family office or regional bank, then a warehouse line from a specialty credit fund once 6 months of loss data exist.
why_now: The program has run since January 1, 2026 and the pain is measured and public (NCPA survey of 500+ owners, SCPC closure warnings). NCPA was still lobbying CMS on faster payment in September 2026 comments on the 2028 guidance, so no fix is in sight. On January 1, 2027 fifteen more drugs, including semaglutide, join and the float grows. The window is roughly the next three to four quarters, before a wholesaler or a bigger lender standardizes an answer.
revenue_model: Discount of about 0.9-1.25% per roughly 3-week cycle on purchased refunds (roughly 15-22% annualized), plus a $250 a month servicing fee per pharmacy. Illustrative unit economics for a pharmacy averaging $400k outstanding: $60-85k gross a year, about $36k cost of funds at 9%, under $6k expected dilution loss, leaving $20-35k contribution. Forty LTC pharmacies is about $16M outstanding and roughly $1M of annual contribution. An association endorsement, not Facebook groups, is affordable CAC at that revenue per account. Later, syndicate or sell seasoned receivables to a credit fund and keep servicing.
non_obvious_insight: LTC is the one segment where the parent's economics and its main risk both improve. Float per logo is 5-30x larger, so one association relationship replaces thousands of low-value retail leads. The dilution mode that worries everyone in retail, 340B lesser-of rejections, should be structurally small because nursing-home residents are rarely patients of 340B covered entities (verify pharmacy by pharmacy). The remaining dilution modes, discharge or death reversals and partial-cycle credits, are predictable from census and cycle-fill data that we ingest and a bank never sees. The lasting asset is a labeled dataset that maps each claim to its refund outcome. Interest is only how it is monetized.
first_30_days: Ask the Senior Care Pharmacy Coalition for introductions to 20 LTC owners and run willingness-to-pay interviews, pricing against 8-12% bank A/R lines and 30%+ MCAs. Sign 5 pharmacies to a free 60-day dilution audit in exchange for claims and remittance files. Build the dilution model in a notebook from those files. Ask the MTF help desk and a healthcare payments attorney what payee-designation options exist. Have a fintech attorney set the true-sale purchase structure, UCC filings and state commercial-financing disclosures. Line up a $500k credit line from a family office or regional bank. Fund the first three advances at $25-50k each with a 25% holdback.
lineage: mutation of I0499 ('Bridge Loans for Medicare Drug-Price Refunds'), type: sharpened
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: SpendMend (MFP Rebate Reconciliation), Plenful (MFP Intelligence / MFP Command Center), ScriptPro Financial Advantage, Liberty Software (and other PMS vendors, e.g. PioneerRx, PrimeRx, Redsail). White space: Verdict: gap, and a narrow one. In roughly 27 searches across varied terms (MFP refund advance, bridge loan, factoring, fintech, PSAO program, wholesaler program) I found NO product that specifically underwrites and advances against MTF-remitted MFP refunds. Pharmacy lenders sell generic A/R and MCA lines, and the MFP players only sell reconciliation. The unserved space is a claim-level underwriting and servicing capability for refund dilution risk: 340B lesser-of rejections (RARC N907 inappropriate rejections), reversals, Good Faith Inquiry disputes, and authorized-generic refund amounts. It is most valuable for borrowers whose float is large: LTC/senior-care pharmacies, 5-50 store groups, and possibly 340B covered entities in the HRSA rebate pilot, where the float is $8.9M-$208M a year for hospitals (Health Affairs). It also applies to the January 2027 step-up when semaglutide joins.

The wedge is weak in five ways.
1. The 'free missing-refund report' is already crowded: SpendMend, Plenful ($76M raised), ScriptPro, Liberty, and free Beacon MFP dashboards.
2. A typical independent's float is small, about $11k a week or $27k a month per NCPA. At 15-25% APR that is roughly $4-7k a year of gross revenue per pharmacy, before losses and a cost of funds of 8-10%. Customer acquisition through state associations and Facebook groups will be costly relative to that.
3. Wholesalers control the payment path. Cardinal routes MFP refunds through Central Pay and wholesalers auto-debit weekly, so a lender's sweep sits behind the wholesaler in practice. Cardinal customers cannot easily direct refunds to a lender-controlled account.
4. 'Non-recourse' is hard to deliver. Manufacturers can reverse refunds and CMS's own materials describe reversals when claims prove ineligible, so a lender will need pharmacy recourse or holdbacks. That undermines the 'prime paper' insight.
5. Policy is a moving target. CMS made manufacturers include cash-flow mitigation plans in their MFP effectuation plans (accelerated refunds, self-identification). NCPA is still pushing CMS and manufacturers for faster payment, including in Sept 2026 comments on the 2028 guidance.

Adjacent generic lenders can also just add MFP refunds to a borrowing base.

Caveat: the WebSearch budget (200 calls) ran out, so Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt and open-source sweeps were not fully run. 'No direct competitor found' means not found, not proven absent. | How this version avoids them: We do not sell reconciliation. SpendMend, Plenful, ScriptPro, Liberty and the free Beacon dashboards all compete on the report. Here the report is an internal underwriting input given away inside the advance, so there is no head-to-head feature race. Plenful targets health systems. Generic pharmacy lenders and Corporate Capital Direct advance against PBM A/R or MCA-style revenue and do not underwrite MFP refunds claim by claim. Live Oak's cheap SBA-style paper funds acquisitions, not a weekly refund float. We complement the senior lender through an intercreditor consent. The wholesaler's payment path, which the parent's research flagged as make-or-break, is handled by payee routing or direct invoice-line payment. That protects the wholesaler's payment, so it has no reason to object. Narrowing to LTC also sidesteps the small-float, high-CAC retail independent.

title: Supplier Watch: Customs Trails Plus Tool Census
one_liner: A supplier-monitoring subscription that reads US customs records for what your factory really ships and to whom, and upgrades to laser-tagged tool census and cavity-fingerprint forensics when the trail looks wrong or a divorce is coming.
customer: US OEMs and PE-owned manufacturers ($50-500M revenue) with $200k-$5M of tooling in China (COO/VP supply chain, with general counsel). Secondary: small and mid-size importers re-sourcing to Vietnam, India, Mexico and Turkey, customs brokers, and factories buying verified credentials.
problem: Brands leaving a Chinese contract manufacturer rarely know which molds and dies they own, or whether the ex-supplier is still running them off the books. Importers of new suppliers can't tell a real factory from a shell. Customs rows tell you who ships what to whom but not what machines exist. A physical audit tells you what tools exist but is expensive and one-time.
solution: Tier 1 is a $2,500 remote 'Supplier Trail + Marketplace Overrun Audit': pull three years of import records for the supplier and its affiliates, find shipments matching the client's product descriptions and codes to consignees other than the client, compare volumes against the client's purchases and plausible capacity, and buy about 10 look-alike units from 1688, Alibaba and Temu to match against the golden sample and lot codes. Tier 2 is Tool Census ($6-15k per site) with a local partner, laser-tagging and cavity fingerprinting. Tier 3 is the forensic evidence pack and tool extraction. Tier 4 is a $149-499 per month watch subscription and a supplier-owned credential for smaller importers and factories.
why_now: Tariff pressure in 2025-26 is pushing brands to move production out of China within the last 24 months, and divorces put tooling at stake exactly when leverage is lowest. LLM parsing of shipping records and computer-vision matching of cavity marks are now cheap enough for a small team.
revenue_model: $2.5k remote audit, $6-15k per Tool Census site, $2-5k per month Overrun Watch per product family, $3-8k per evidence pack, 8-12% of appraised tool value on extraction, $149-499 per month and $150-400 per dossier for smaller importers, and $600-1,200 per year factory credentials. Expected first-year ACV for a manufacturer is $40-120k.
non_obvious_insight: The customs trail lets you run forensics remotely before anyone flies to China, since an ex-supplier shipping your part number to a third consignee shows up in the record as a shipper-consignee pair with volume. Conversely, every confirmed overrun case is a rare labeled positive for the anomaly model, which is otherwise unlabeled and generic like ImportGenius, and the census provides ground-truth capacity to sanity-check shipping volumes. The cheap watch subscription also identifies which suppliers are about to become the high-ticket cases.
first_30_days: Buy 12 months of import records for two categories and auto-build about 1,000 factory profiles, hand-auditing 20. Sell the $2,500 remote audit to 3 design partners through Ohio plant-manager and Reshoring Initiative networks. Line up a Dongguan or Ningbo audit contractor by referral and book an hour with an IP litigator who will white-label the evidence-pack format. Send 200 emails to sourcing managers and customs brokers for the watch subscription.
lineage: hybrid of I0552 + I1209 (Supplier Divorce Protection: Tool Census and Overrun Forensics + Real-Factory Credentials From Customs Shipping Records). Why stronger: Tool Census alone is a high-ticket, low-frequency service with a long sales cycle, and customs credentials alone compete directly with ImportGenius, Panjiva and ImportYeti. Together, the cheap subscription is the funnel to the expensive census, the census and forensics supply ground truth that makes the credential defensible, and forensic cases keep improving the anomaly model.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Harris Sliwoski (China Law Blog), Alitheon (FeaturePrint), Red Points, Corsearch (Zeal 2.0, Investigations 360, Distribution Control). White space: Coverage caveat: the WebSearch quota (200 per session) was already used up when I started, so I could not run the planned 6-12 searches. I also could not check Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt, TechCrunch or open-source repos. The findings below come from about 25 direct page fetches, so treat 'nobody does this' as unproven. The vendors most likely missed are the many small China-based QC and sourcing agents that sell 'mold audits' and 'mold relocation', plus PI and investigation firms (Kroll-type). Do a manual pass on those before committing.

What I found: I found no productized, US-facing service that bundles (a) a serialized tool census, (b) cavity-level physical fingerprints, and (c) marketplace test-buy attribution of overruns to a specific tool. The problem is documented and treated as an unproductized legal-advice problem: Harris Sliwoski tells clients to keep an inventory form and audit quarterly, and never mentions a third-party vendor for it. Marketplace monitoring and takedown (Red Points, Corsearch, Alibaba's free IP platform) is commoditized and crowded. Object fingerprinting exists (Alitheon) but is aimed at electronics, aerospace and gray-market diversion, not tool-mark attribution.

Genuinely unserved: (1) cavity-level 'which tool made this part' attribution that holds up as evidence; (2) a tooling census standard for mid-market OEMs, timed to the exit window; (3) an evidence pack designed for counsel that a brand-protection vendor's screenshot-and-takedown workflow does not produce.

Weak points: Extraction (tool 3) is freight, customs and re-qualification work that sourcing agents and forwarders already do at low margin. Monitoring (tool 2, first half) is a commodity. Attribution is legally useful only when the overrun carries the client's IP (trademark, design patent, trade dress) and the client can enforce it. If the part is generic or unbranded, a match proves little. Chinese-court enforceability is unproven here. || Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: ImportGenius, Panjiva (S&P Global Market Intelligence), Descartes Datamyne, ImportYeti. White space: The narrow wedge that appears unserved is a fixed-price, human-reviewed 'reasonable-care file' for a small US importer, sold through customs brokers. The SMB importer (Amazon or Shopify brand, or a $2-50M distributor) needs one factory checked before one PO. Enterprise tools (Sayari, Altana, Tradeverifyd, Trademo, Exiger) are sold by demo and are priced and scoped for large compliance teams. Data tools (ImportGenius, Panjiva, Datamyne, ImportYeti) sell rows and leave interpretation to the analyst. Inspectors (QIMA) and sourcing agents (Sourcify) sell physical checks, not a documentary file that maps to CBP's reasonable-care standard. The part I found nobody offering is a factory-claimed profile with consent-based buyer references, which is a two-sided credential. No visible player runs a supplier-owned reputation credential built on customs ledgers. However, the wedge is thin. (1) ImportGenius already markets 'supplier verification via shipping history' at the same $229-449/mo price band. (2) The raw-data floor is free or near-free. (3) Any one of Altana, Trademo or ImportGenius could add a 'transshipment risk report' feature quickly. (4) The factory-pays credential side has no demonstrated demand and needs a two-sided marketplace. Risks I could not check with the exhausted search budget: whether resale of licensed bill-of-lading data is allowed, that US import records often name the forwarder or trading company as shipper instead of the factory, that importers can request confidentiality under 19 CFR 103.31, and that no CBP safe-harbor exists for third-party dossiers.

title: Independent Big-Meter Audits With Refund Guarantee
one_liner: A brand-neutral audit of a utility's 100-400 largest meters: AMI history is turned into a ranked, field-tested list of under-registering accounts. It is sold as a fixed-price small purchase, refunded if verified annual recovery is under 2x the fee.
customer: Finance director or utility director at a combined water+sewer municipal utility with 10-40k connections. AMI (or monthly-read AMR) is fully deployed, there are 100-400 meters of 3 inch and larger, and there is no in-house crew to bench- or field-test large meters. A rate hearing or rate study is due within 9 months. Wedge accounts: hospitals, hotels, food and beverage plants, universities and laundries. These run all night on low flows, which is exactly where old compound and turbine meters under-read.
problem: The parent's ghost-parcel half is weak (permits trigger taps, ADUs are usually billed on a shared meter) and contingency contracts are restricted or slow in some states. Back-billing is legally capped and politically toxic. The real leak is quieter. The utility's most valuable meters are 15-30 years old and lose low-flow registration. The meter is also the instrument that would have to report its own failure. Every under-read gallon is lost twice, because sewer charges on commercial accounts are billed off the water read. Councils are approving 5-10% rate steps while nobody has tested the top-revenue meters. Meter vendors and distributors do test large meters, but their business is selling the replacement.
solution: Step 1: get one CSV of 24 months of reads or interval data for the top 100-400 accounts, plus the meter inventory (size, make, install year). Step 2: compute a 'low-flow fingerprint' per account: (a) share of hours with zero registered flow versus use-code and NAICS peers that show base load; (b) a hole in the flow histogram just below the compound-meter crossover or start-up flow; (c) step-downs after meter or endpoint changes; (d) zero-read or estimated-read streaks. Step 3: rank by expected annual dollars, water plus sewer. Step 4: an independent crew field-tests the top 12-15 (three flow rates, AWWA M6-style, in-situ rig) and issues test certificates. Step 5: deliver a council-ready 2-page brief ('this recovers $X a year and offsets Y points of the next rate step'), a brand-neutral replacement spec, and prospective-only correction as the default. Recovery comes from swapping the meter, not from back-billing. The measured under-registration also replaces the default assumption in the utility's AWWA/M36 water audit and raises its Data Validity Score.
why_now: Utilities that finished AMI in 2018-2022 now hold 4+ years of hourly data that no one has analyzed for revenue. PFAS, lead-line and pipe capex are forcing rate hikes into affordability fights, so 'prove we've fixed our own leaks first' is a strong council story. State water-audit mandates (for example Texas for systems with 3,300+ connections) create an annual moment when apparent losses are examined. Cheap data engineering means a two-person team can build the fingerprint model. Incumbent meter makers have no credible way to tell a customer that their installed base under-registers.
revenue_model: Fixed fee of about $24k (scan plus 12 independent tests), priced under typical small-purchase or informal-bid limits (to verify per state), refunded in full if verified annualized recoverable revenue is under 2x the fee. Add-ons: $1.5k per meter for post-swap verification; an annual 'Big Meter Monitor' at $8-15k a year per utility; licensing the screen to rate consultants and AMI vendors. An opt-in success share applies only in states where it is lawful, for ghost-parcel or sewer-only leads. Assumed unit economics: about $10k COGS per audit (about 30 analyst hours, 12 subcontracted tests at roughly $600-800). About 55-60% gross margin and about 30 audits a year for two people is roughly $700k, before monitor ARR.
non_obvious_insight: A refund guarantee on a fixed fee gets the benefits of contingency (zero risk, easy yes) without the parts that block contingency: percentage-of-recovery bans, RFP thresholds and 'paid to find money' optics. The defensible asset is not the model. It is a private labeled dataset of field-test accuracy by meter make, model, size and age matched to its AMI fingerprint. Only a party with no meters to sell can collect it, and each audit adds about 12 ground-truth labels. Recovery is mostly prospective, so the back-billing fight in the parent version never happens.
first_30_days: Pull the 'principal water customers' table from five target utilities' public annual financial reports and the state rate-study calendar. Pick 15 utilities with 10-40k connections and a hearing in the next 9 months. Offer a free 5-business-day screen of the top 100 accounts from one CSV. Line up a test-rig subcontractor and an AWWA-experienced water-loss advisor. Test the top 3 leads at the first free screen for free, using the findings as the proof case. Pre-sell one paid audit with the guarantee to a utility whose hearing is scheduled. Confirm the small-purchase limit in the first two states. Also test the unverified claim that large meters are 40-60% of revenue by checking the annual financial reports.
lineage: mutation of I0388 ('Contingency Hunters for Unbilled Water Revenue'), type: sharpened
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Itron (Temetra Analysis / Non-Revenue Water portfolio), Badger Meter (BEACON, OneNetwork), Master Meter (Harmony Encore MDM), Metron-Farnier (WaterScope). White space: Important caveat: my WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200) before any of my searches ran. This verdict rests on about 20 direct page fetches and GitHub repo searches, not on broad web, Crunchbase, YC or Product Hunt sweeps. Treat 'no direct competitor found' as unconfirmed, and do a manual pass on Crunchbase, YC and RFP portals before committing. (2) The metering and analytics incumbents (Itron, Badger, Master Meter, Metron) sell software tied to their own hardware, with no evidence of a ranked, dollar-denominated, legal-ready recovery list or contingency pricing. title: Rotor Rescue as Scrapyard Deal-Sourcing Engine
one_liner: Use the pay-per-rotor magnet program as the free-to-yard front door that surfaces retiring scrapyard owners and gives search-fund buyers a day-one margin lever and guaranteed magnet supply.

Rotor Rescue's scarce inputs are trust with thousands of skeptical independent yards and aggregate volume, and recyclers such as Cyclic already court suppliers directly.
solution: Phase 1: run Rotor Rescue in 2-3 states with a loaner gauss meter and a price sheet by motor model, paying yards per unit and aggregating lots for recyclers. Each enrolled yard reveals throughput, mix and owner age, so the program flags retirement-age owners. Phase 2: cohort members get first look at flagged yards, a permit-transfer and environmental diligence pack, SBA-lender introductions, and a ready 'magnet program' they can run on day one in the acquired yard. First sellable product: cohort seats at $4-6K that include the Rotor Rescue playbook and pre-sourced sell-side LOIs.
why_now: AI-driven hiring freezes are producing capable managers with cash and time. Greenfield battery and plastics recycling is failing (Ascend Elements and Li-Cycle bankruptcies), while permitted, cash-flowing yards look safe. DOE announced $134M for critical-mineral demonstrations in June 2026, and DoD-backed magnet plants create domestic pull and funded recyclers that need feed.
revenue_model: Cohort tuition of $4-6K per seat. Buy-side success fee of $25-50K or 1.5-2% at close. 2-5% advisory equity in each acquisition. Sell-side listing fees from retiring owners. Spread on assayed magnet feed sold to recyclers, plus a small SaaS fee for the identification and price app. Diligence-pack licensing to lenders.

Retiring owners rarely list with brokers; they tell whoever already writes them checks. That makes Rotor Rescue a proprietary deal-sourcing channel disguised as a price-discovery service. In the other direction, an owned portfolio of yards turns the magnet-feed aggregation problem into contracted supply, which a national recycler would rather buy from than chase yard by yard.

title: Tool Passport: Molds That Report Themselves
one_liner: An OEM-owned, tamper-evident magnetic cycle counter and registry that makes every mold or die report its own location and shot count, so an unauthorized overrun shows up on the owner's screen and, in time, verified tools can be financed and insured.
customer: Wedge: US OEMs and PE-owned manufacturers ($50M-$500M) that have just moved, or are moving, tools out of China to US, Mexican, Vietnamese or Indian molders and never want a second breakup. Second user: the receiving nearshore molder, who installs the tag to earn 'verified' status with skittish customers. Later payers: tooling lenders, insurers and procurement teams that require a Passport.
problem: Even after reshoring, the OEM's tools sit in someone else's building with no independent record of how many shots they have run, on which press or when. The molder's own counters and MES data are self-reported. Enforcement is all after-the-fact forensics, which is expensive and easy to dispute. Because tools cannot be verified, they are worth nothing as collateral, cannot be insured on custody, and force OEMs into blunt contracts with minimum order quantities and amortization games.
solution: Phase 1 product, 'Tool Heartbeat', is a magnet-mount IP67 tag with an accelerometer that counts mold-open and mold-close cycles from vibration signatures, geofences the tool, detects removal, stores and forwards data over LTE-M, and reports to a per-tool 'passport': QR plate, serial, photo and fingerprint baseline, custody chain, shot ledger versus POs. Silence is contractually a breach. A model 'Tool Passport Addendum' for MSAs, drafted with a China-facing law firm, gives the OEM tag access and audit rights. Phase 2 uses the ledger as the meter for pay-per-shot billing and escrow, so the molder is paid per verified shot and proves innocence. Phase 3 is the registry as a standard: a VIN-and-Carfax for tools that lenders accept for collateral and underwriters use for custody cover. Phase 4 is Passport-backed tooling finance and custody insurance, where the balance-sheet upside sits. Tools still in China get the Census-and-forensics service from the parent, not tags, until SIM roaming and consent barriers are solved.
why_now: Reshoring has created thousands of just-moved tools whose owners are motivated to prevent a repeat. LTE-M and NB-IoT modules with IMUs now cost roughly $25-45 in BOM for a 3-5 year tag. EUROMAP 77 / OPC UA 40077 machine interfaces make molder-side data available to cross-check the independent witness. The tariff-driven wave of moves in 2025-26 (per the parent research) means a stock of new supplier relationships where the tag can be built into the contract from day one.
revenue_model: Hardware $150 per tag (roughly 60% margin at scale), $10 per tool per month for the ledger and alerts, and $1,000 per site onboarding (QR plates, fingerprint baseline, custody paperwork). A 60-tool OEM pays about $22k in year one and $7k a year after. Reaching $1M ARR takes about 140 OEM-sites, so the early business is small. The upside is in the standard: verified-tool finance fees and custody insurance premiums, plus a 'Passport Verified' seal for molders. This is a longer-dated bet, and the near-term money rests on services and hardware.
non_obvious_insight: The parent asks how to prove theft afterward. The inversion is that a tool is the only expensive asset in manufacturing that reports nothing about itself. A cycle count is a signal the tool already produces every 30 seconds through its own vibration, and no one owns it as a customer-side record. Once an independent meter exists, the honest molder benefits as much as the OEM, because it settles quantity disputes, proves clean custody and lets the molder offer pay-per-shot pricing. That aligned incentive is what makes a standard plausible, where a policing tool would not spread.
first_30_days: Weeks 1-3: build 10 prototype tags from an off-the-shelf LTE-M module and IMU (Blues Notecard-class) in a magnetic housing, about $3k. Validate cycle-count accuracy (target within 1%) on 2-3 presses at a friendly Ohio molder who gets free tags and 'Passport-ready' status. Weeks 2-4: pre-sell 3 OEM pilots at $2,400 for 10 tags plus a year of service with a refundable deposit, using the Reshoring Initiative and Ohio plant-manager networks. Draft the Addendum with one law firm. Use the $2,500 Marketplace Overrun Audit as the top-of-funnel cross-sell. Kill signal: vibration counting cannot reach 98% accuracy across press types, or fewer than 2 of 10 OEMs will sign a pilot.

title: Neutral Registry and Standard for Neighbor Baselines
one_liner: An independent, vendor-agnostic registry and open protocol that notarizes pre-construction baselines from any sensor vendor or consultant, gets referenced in county ordinances and a model presumption statute, and becomes the title-plant-style record that insurers and lenders underwrite against.
customer: Three payers, sequenced. (1) Sensor vendors and developer-hired consultancies (KETOS, Aethair, Kunak resellers, TRC and Salas O'Brien-type firms) that need a neutral stamp so counties will believe their data. (2) Data center developers who must file a baseline to satisfy an ordinance or a hearing (50-500 MW campuses in contested counties). (3) Later, insurers, lenders and state agencies buying registry data and certification. Counties and regulators are the standard's adopters, not payers.
problem: Every county and agency is inventing its own baseline rules: a 48-hour ambient sound survey here, monitoring wells and a hydrogeologist there (Franklin County IN, Chadds Ford PA, Shenandoah VA, St. Louis, Virginia DEQ's five Kunak sensors in Loudoun). Developer-hired consultants produce the data, so residents distrust it; opposition-side groups produce competing data, so developers distrust that. Nothing makes a baseline tamper-evident, comparable across sites, or legally meaningful. Unlike Pennsylvania's Act 13 for oil and gas (operators pay for pre-drill tests, and a rebuttable presumption applies when no baseline exists), no data-center equivalent creates a legal reason to buy, which is the parent's biggest unproven assumption.
solution: Build the audit-firm layer for baselines, in four steps. (1) Protocol v1, open and free: sensor siting rules, control-site design, QA/QC, minimum 90 days pre-application, chain of custody and data schema for wells, noise, PM2.5 and voltage, written with a land-grant university hydrogeologist and an acoustician. (2) The registry: any vendor submits raw data through an API, and we run automated QA, protocol audit and dual-key custody (a university library or state geological survey as second custodian, plus RFC 3161-style public timestamp logs, no token). The output is a Registered Baseline certificate with tamper-evident, first-in timestamps and a public read-only view. (3) The adoption engine: a one-page ordinance rider ('baseline must be registered under an independent public-benefit protocol') sent to every county drafting rules, and a model bill for the January 2027 legislative sessions (TX and NY are the pressure points) that adapts the Act 13 logic: a registered baseline lets a developer rebut unsupported claims, while no registered baseline shifts the presumption to the operator. (4) Governance: a public-benefit board with county, university, developer and resident seats, so no vendor controls it. Year 2-3 balance-sheet option: once 30+ campuses are registered, use the loss-relevant data to launch a developer-owned risk retention group or mutual for neighbor-harm guarantees, with the registry as its underwriting file. The same registry then extends to other large-load neighbors (battery storage, fabs, lithium, hydrogen).
why_now: The moratorium wave (NY EO 62 on July 14, Texas TCEQ halt on Sept 21, local pauses) means regulators must define 'what evidence counts' before lifting pauses. State legislatures convene in January 2027. Counties are copy-pasting bespoke baseline language right now, so an early standard can be the copied text. Public-sector baselines are starting (Virginia DEQ's Loudoun air sensors since Feb 2026) and need tamper-evident custody, and the Newton County lawsuit (Sept 2026) is a live example of dueling studies. Sensor prices collapsed, so the scarce input is now trust, not data.
revenue_model: Registry filing fee of $15-25k per site (protocol audit, QA, dual-key custody, certificate) plus $3-6k per year custody for 10 years; vendor and assessor certification of about $10k per firm per year for the registry-verified listing; data and API licences to insurers, lenders, state agencies and researchers; later, a premium share if a mutual launches. Bottom-up sketch: 150 new registrations per year at $20k = $3M; 500 custodied sites at $4.5k = $2.25M; 60 certified firms at $10k = $0.6M; about $6M per year by year 3 from data centers alone, with the upside from adjacent industries and underwriting data. Sales-cycle proxy: a filing is a line item in a permit budget, not a new budget.
non_obvious_insight: The incumbents are the channel, not the enemy. Developer-hired consultants and sensor vendors already produce the baselines but cannot be believed, and their best sales asset is a credible neutral attestation, exactly as companies prepare their own books but need an independent auditor to be trusted. So the registry sells to the competitors' customers through the competitors, and vendors pay to be certified because counties will ask for it. The moat is a cornered resource (first-in timestamped pre-construction baselines cannot be recreated after a site is built), network economies (cross-site data improves control models and expected-loss estimates) and switching costs (10-year custody), backed by counter-positioning (a vendor cannot be neutral without giving up its own product). The lever that decides everything is the legal presumption, which is why the model bill and ordinance rider are part of the product, not lobbying on the side.
first_30_days: Days 1-14: draft Protocol v0.1 with a land-grant extension hydrogeologist and an independent acoustician; publish it CC-BY with a one-page ordinance rider. Days 10-25: send the rider to the county attorneys behind Franklin County IN, Shenandoah VA, Chadds Ford PA and 10 other counties with open drafts; ask to be named as an acceptable registry. Days 15-30: sign 3-5 letters of intent from sensor vendors and consultancies to submit pilot baselines for the Registered Baseline certificate; book calls with two state association-of-counties or legislative staff on presumption language for TX and NY. Sell the first two filings ($12-18k pilot pricing) to developers with hearings in the next 60-90 days. Six-month target: 10 registered sites, 3 vendors certified, one ordinance or permit condition naming the registry, $150-250k of fees. Gate: if no county or regulator will reference the protocol within 6 months, fall back to selling attestations as a service inside the well-trustee model (offspring 1).
lineage: mutation of I1172 ('Neutral Baselines and Neighbor Guarantees for Data Centers'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: KETOS (SHIELD / KELP data-center water monitoring), Aethair (Aethair PRO, Environet, Thiamis), Envirosuite (ASX:EVS), Kunak. White space: Nobody found sells the bundle, so the status is 'gap' and not 'open'. The sensor and baseline layer is not open: KETOS (about $45M raised) pitches an independent baseline for data centers, Aethair pitches pre-construction baselines, Envirosuite has community dashboards, and consultancies bundle baselines into permitting. The unserved wedge is what sits on top of the sensors. (1) A neutral administrator holding escrowed, tamper-evident data whose governance the county and community accept, unlike developer-hired consultants and unlike opposition-side groups such as CEDS. (2) The Neighbor Guarantee: an automatic, no-litigation payout to households from a developer-funded escrow when a pre-agreed trigger is hit. No vendor, insurer, county ordinance or developer program found does this. The nearest things are Franklin County, Indiana's draft rule (escrow for 24-hour emergency potable water to impacted neighbors, plus developer-funded monitoring wells), one-off buyouts and lump-sum checks. (3) A 10-year, multi-parameter (wells, noise, PM2.5, voltage) record packaged as a permit-condition template that regulators can adopt. Weak points: the sensor baseline will commoditize; attribution is hard, because well drawdown from drought or other pumping is indistinguishable from data-center drawdown unless the design uses upgradient control wells and pumping records; automatic payouts may look like insurance under state law; and developer counsel may resist a pre-committed payout as an admission of liability. Note: the web-search budget ran out before I could check Crunchbase/YC directly for a startup doing exactly the escrow-plus-parametric bundle, so 'nobody found' means no evidence in about 25 searches, not proof of absence. | How this version avoids them: It does not compete with KETOS, Aethair, Kunak, Clarity, Larson Davis or Eno on hardware or dashboards; they submit data and pay to be verified, so their marketing (KETOS's 'missing baseline', Aethair's pre-construction guide) creates our demand. Envirosuite, the strongest incumbent, sells recurring monitoring SaaS to sites that pay it and cannot credibly be the independent notary of its own customers' data. Consultancies (TRC, Salas O'Brien, Trinity, SCS) are developer-hired and gain from a stamp that makes their work believed. CEDS advises opposition groups and is not neutral, but its recommended pre-, during- and post-construction baselines match our protocol, so it is a natural endorser.
